title: The Ark Comes Up the Right Way
summary: David prepares a tent for the ark in Jerusalem and this time insists that only the Levites carry it, as Moses commanded. He gathers the priests and Levitical clans, has them consecrate themselves, and appoints singers and musicians. The ark is brought up with sacrifice, music, and shouting, while Saul's daughter Michal watches David dance and despises him.
story: Three months earlier, David's first attempt to move the ark ended when Uzzah touched it and died (1 Chronicles 13). Chapter 14 showed that God was still establishing David. Now David tries again, and this chapter is about the difference between the two attempts. The first time, the ark rode on a new cart, as the Philistines had once sent it (1 Samuel 6), and no one consulted the law. This time David has learned. The ark goes up on Levite shoulders, the priests are consecrated, and the procession is organized around worship. The chapter prepares for the installation of the ark in chapter 16 and, further off, for the temple that Solomon will build, where the Levites and musicians named here will serve.
historical:
The ark had been neglected through Saul's reign (13:3). Captured by the Philistines in the days of Eli (1 Samuel 4), returned, and left for decades at Kiriath-jearim, it had been apart from the tabernacle, which by David's time stood at Gibeon (16:39). By bringing the ark to Jerusalem, the city he had just taken, David made his capital the religious center of all the tribes. This was also a political act, since no Israelite tribe had held Jerusalem before, but the Chronicler's interest lies in its meaning for worship.

Chronicles was written after the return from exile in Babylon, most likely in the Persian period around 400 to 350 BC, though some date it a little earlier or later. Its first readers had a rebuilt temple and working Levitical orders but no king. The long lists of Levites and musicians here gave them roots: the worship they practiced reached back to David's own ordering of it.
cultural:
The ark of the covenant was a gold-covered wooden chest holding the tablets of the covenant, described in Exodus 25 as the place above which God would meet with his people. It was fitted with poles so that it could be carried without being touched. Numbers 4 and 7:9 assign the carrying of the holy things to the Kohathite Levites, on their shoulders, and Numbers 4:15 warns that touching them brings death. The Levites were the tribe descended from Levi, set apart for the service of the sanctuary; the priests were the branch of Levi descended from Aaron. The six clan heads in verses 5-10 include the three great divisions of Levi (Kohath, Merari, Gershom) and three prominent Kohathite subclans (Elizaphan, Hebron, Uzziel).

The musical instruments are the ordinary ones of Israel's worship: harps and lyres (stringed instruments of different sizes), cymbals, trumpets, and the ram's horn. The terms Alamoth and Sheminith in verses 20-21 also appear in psalm titles (Psalm 46, Psalms 6 and 12). Their meaning is uncertain. Alamoth may relate to the word for young women, suggesting a high register, and Sheminith means the eighth, which some take as a lower octave or an eight-stringed instrument. The linen ephod David wears was a priestly garment, and his wearing it signals the king taking part in worship, not claiming to be a priest.
literary: This chapter is built around David's explanation in verse 13, which names the lesson of the Uzzah story. Around it the Chronicler places what the lesson produced: a careful assembly (verses 1-11), consecration (verses 12-15), the appointment of musicians and gatekeepers (verses 16-24), and the joyful procession (verses 25-28). The lists are not filler. They are the evidence that worship was now being done in the right order. The chapter closes with a single verse about Michal (verse 29), taken from 2 Samuel 6:16. The Chronicler omits the longer quarrel between David and Michal found in 2 Samuel 6:20-23, but the single glance from the window is enough. In the middle of joy there is contempt, and it comes from the house of Saul, whose failure to seek God began the book's story of David.

outline.t: David prepares a place and gathers Israel
The Levitical clans and their leaders
The lesson learned: consecration and the Levites' shoulders
The ark brought up with rejoicing

doctrines.note: God's presence is a gift, but it is not safe to handle carelessly. David admits the disaster came because they did not consult Him about the proper order (verse 13). Holiness shapes how worship is done, and reverence and joy stand side by side in this chapter.

The ark is carried as Moses had commanded in accordance with the word of the LORD (verse 15). The Chronicler's point is that good intentions did not replace obedience to what God had already revealed.

Worship here is corporate and ordered: the elders, the commanders, the priests, the Levites, and all Israel each have a part. The Chronicler presents the gathered people praising God together as the heart of Israel's life.

words.note: Mishpat, usually justice or judgment, but here the proper order or prescribed way (verse 13). The word covers what is right in a court and what is right in a ritual. David's confession is that they did not seek God about the right procedure. The same word will later describe God's judgments in the psalm of chapter 16.

Qadash, to consecrate or make holy. Priests and Levites set themselves apart before handling the ark (verses 12 and 14), which in the law involved washing and ritual purity. The word marks the move from the common to the holy and is the root of the word for holiness.

Simchah, joy or rejoicing. The singers raise their voices with joy (verse 16), and David and the leaders go with rejoicing (verse 25). Chronicles pairs careful order with exuberant gladness; obedience is not presented as joyless.
Darash, to seek or consult. It is the Chronicler's signature word for turning to God. In verse 13 its absence is the problem: we did not consult Him. The same verb described Saul's failure in 10:14.

christ: The ark was the throne-chest of God's presence among his people, carried with fear and joy. The New Testament uses the language of God dwelling with his people for Jesus himself: John says the Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us (John 1:14), using a verb related to the tabernacle. The letter to the Hebrews presents Christ as the high priest who enters God's presence on our behalf, so that believers may approach with confidence rather than dread. That confidence doesn't cancel the holiness this chapter teaches; it rests on a mediator who has made the approach right. The connection is thematic and typological, a pattern that the New Testament develops, not a prediction within the chapter.

hard.q: Was God unfair to strike Uzzah, and does this chapter blame him or David?
hard.a: Uzzah's death (1 Chronicles 13) strikes many readers as harsh: he reached out to steady the ark with apparently good motives. This chapter gives David's own verdict in verse 13. The fault lay with the whole leadership, David included, for ignoring the law's clear instructions about who should carry the ark and how. Some interpreters stress that the holy things were explicitly guarded by the death penalty (Numbers 4:15), so the event was a known danger, not an arbitrary one. Others stress that the story teaches the seriousness of God's presence at a founding moment, much as Nadab and Abihu's deaths did at the tabernacle's beginning (Leviticus 10). The difficulty doesn't vanish, but the chapter presents a king who takes responsibility rather than blaming God or Uzzah, and who returns with reverence instead of giving up.

questions: David's first attempt failed not from bad motives but from not asking how God wanted it done. Where might good intentions be standing in for listening?
The chapter holds careful order and wild joy together. Which of the two comes more easily to you or your church, and what would the other add?
Michal watched from a window and despised what she saw. What keeps people at a distance from worship, criticizing instead of joining?
